mcqs.question: An engineer spends a full day on a one-time, never-seen-before production investigation. Does this count as toil?
options: No, because toil specifically requires the work to be repetitive, and a novel one-time investigation fails that test
Yes, because it's manual, hands-on work
Yes, because it took an entire day
No, because toil only applies to work done by junior engineers
mcqs.explanation: Toil requires manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical work with no lasting value — a genuinely novel investigation isn't repetitive, so it doesn't qualify even though it's manual and time-consuming. Duration and seniority of the person doing it aren't part of the definition.

mcqs.question: On the automation ladder, what's the key difference between the "scripted" rung and the "self-service" rung?
options: Scripted work requires no human at all, while self-service still needs the on-call engineer
Scripted still requires the on-call engineer to run the script; self-service lets the requester trigger it directly without paging anyone
They're the same thing, just different names
Self-service is only used for security-sensitive tasks, scripted is used everywhere else
mcqs.explanation: A script alone still requires someone (typically on-call) to execute it — the toil is reduced but not eliminated for that person. Self-service removes even that step by letting the original requester trigger the automation themselves, with no on-call involvement.

mcqs.question: Why does Google's SRE model cap toil-like work at roughly 50% of an SRE's time instead of relying on teams to reduce it organically?
options: Because 50% is a legal requirement for on-call staffing
Because SREs are only allowed to work half-time
Because toil tends to expand to fill all available time otherwise, so a hard cap forces automation work to actually get scheduled
Because it guarantees zero incidents will occur
mcqs.explanation: Left unmanaged, there's always another urgent manual task competing for time, so toil left to teams' good intentions tends to consume all available hours. A hard cap is a forcing function that protects time for the automation work that actually reduces future toil — it's not a legal rule, a part-time mandate, or a reliability guarantee.

mcqs.question: What's the risk of automating a manual process before questioning whether the process itself should exist?
options: There's no risk — automation always improves any process
It's only risky if the automation uses a scripting language rather than a compiled one
It always increases the team's toil rather than reducing it
It locks in and speeds up a wasteful or even risky process instead of removing it, making the underlying issue harder to notice
mcqs.explanation: Automating a step whose purpose no one has re-examined can fossilize waste or quietly remove a safeguard, running it faster and more invisibly rather than fixing anything. The fix is to question necessity first, then simplify, then automate — not to assume automation is always a pure improvement regardless of what it's automating.
